subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Narrow Framing and Broad Framing
description: One-minute skill: Narrow Framing and Broad Framing.

hook.text: Offered one coin flip for $200 or nothing, you decline. Offered 100 such flips, you accept immediately.

buildup.text: Narrow framing evaluates each gamble individually. Broad framing aggregates them into a portfolio.

discovery.text: Loss aversion makes each individual bet feel painful. But a bundle of bets nearly guarantees a profit overall.

twist.text: Investors who check portfolios daily lose more than those who check yearly.

climax.text: Zoom out. Evaluate decisions as part of a lifetime of decisions, not as isolated events. Broad framing reduces fear.

punchline.text: One bet is scary. A hundred bets are safe.

quiz.question: Why does checking investments daily lead to worse decisions?
options: Markets are always down in the morning
Narrow framing increases the pain of individual losses

details.summary: Narrow framing evaluates each decision in isolation, while broad framing considers the aggregate effect of many decisions together. Loss aversion is strongest under narrow framing because each individual loss feels painful even if the portfolio of decisions is profitable overall.
details.whyItMatters: Investors who check portfolios daily experience more loss aversion than those who check annually, because narrow framing exposes them to individual daily losses. Broader evaluation periods reduce the emotional impact of volatility.
takeaways: Narrow framing amplifies loss aversion by isolating each decision
Broad framing reduces loss aversion by aggregating outcomes
Checking investments less frequently can improve decision quality

faq.question: Why do frequent portfolio checks lead to worse decisions?
faq.answer: Daily stock prices go down almost as often as up. Each downtick triggers loss aversion pain. Investors who check daily experience more pain than pleasure over time and sell good investments prematurely to stop the discomfort.

faq.question: How can you use broad framing to make better decisions?
faq.answer: Consider decisions as part of a lifetime portfolio rather than isolated events. Accept that some individual decisions will lose money if the overall strategy is sound. Reduce the frequency of checking outcomes to avoid narrow framing.
